title: Guru Granth, Guru Panth
hook: he left the Guru's authority to the scripture and to the Khalsa gathered before it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanded: the river in the south where the Tenth Guru's road ended. Your line was the last days. What did you settle? Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

Who comes next? Communities that lose a leader ask it. Families ask it over a will. Companies ask it in a boardroom. For nearly every step of Sikh history so far, the answer had been a person: Guru Nanak passed the light to Guru Angad, and on down the line, ten Gurus in all. At Nanded, with his time running out, the Tenth Guru was asked the same question. Sikhs remember his answer as a turning point. It wasn't a name.
screen: `WHO COMES NEXT?` → `ALWAYS, UNTIL NOW, A PERSON.` → `THIS TIME, NOT A NAME.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh placed the Guru's authority in two places at once. First, the scripture. The book of the Gurus' hymns, the Adi Granth, would itself be the Guru from now on: the Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means a book, a volume. Second, the people. The Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs, gathered in the presence of that book, would carry the Guru's authority together: the Guru Panth. Panth means a path, and the people who walk it. A verse Sikhs sing after the Ardas, the common prayer, carries this memory. In paraphrase: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was founded; let every Sikh accept the Granth as the Guru. You can see the two halves fit. The book holds the word. The people, gathered before it, decide how to live it. Neither stands alone. That's why, in a gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is treated not as a library book but as a living Guru: opened in the morning under a canopy, a whisk waved over it, carried to rest at night. And it's why important matters for the Panth have been decided by Sikhs meeting together in the Guru's presence, sometimes through five chosen Sikhs who stand for the whole Khalsa. It is a bold answer. No single successor to argue over. No one person who could be bribed or killed. The Guru's word is fixed in a book anyone can open, and the authority to apply it belongs to a gathered community. The line of ten ends, and the Guru goes on.
screen: `THE BOOK BECOMES THE GURU.` · `THE GATHERED KHALSA, THE GURU PANTH.` · `THE WORD, AND THE PEOPLE WHO LIVE IT.` · `NO SINGLE SUCCESSOR TO FIGHT OVER.` · then, large: `THE BOOK AND THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor both. Settle, and breathe. First, the book. Bring to mind the words that have guided you, from any page that has mattered, and simply bow your head a little toward them. Then, the people. Picture the circle you belong to, family, friends, a congregation, a team, and hold them in your mind with respect. Rest between the two. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for each. The bell holds the time.
Guru Granth. The scripture as living Guru, given that authority, tradition says, by Guru Gobind Singh, alongside the gathered Khalsa, the Guru Panth. Today's word.
Your line: the book and the people. Today, when you make a choice, check it twice: against the words you trust, and with someone you trust. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is installed each morning under a canopy and laid to rest at night, and Sikhs gathered before it decide matters for the community together; a verse sung after the Ardas recalls the Granth as Guru.

original.note: Punjabi: a book, a volume. With Guru, the scripture as the living Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs have a holy book.
what it means: the book itself is the Guru, and the gathered Khalsa carries the Guru's authority with it.
what a scholar hears: a turn from personal succession to a shared authority of word and community, remembered in a verse sung after the Ardas.

notes: The hook says 'ten Gurus in all'; this is standard Sikh teaching but is a count, please confirm it is acceptable under the claims rule.
The paraphrase of the verse sung after Ardas ('agya bhai akal ki... sab sikhan ko hukam hai guru manyo granth') is loose; please check wording and how to attribute its origin.
Glosses of granth (a book) and panth (a path, and the people on it) are common; please confirm.
The description of decisions made in the Guru's presence, sometimes through five chosen Sikhs (panj pyare), is general; please confirm framing.
